newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi sees mayor relying on risky fiscal plan.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi sees mayor relying on risky fiscal plan.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi warned Tuesday that the Giuliani Administration's proposed budget for fiscal year 1998 had big risks and relied on maneuvers that did not come through this year.

Hevesi highlighted the city's dependence on Wall Street banks and brokerage houses, whose more than $11 billion of estimated profits for calendar 1996 are expected to give both New York City and New York State large surpluses in fiscal 1997.
The city's watchdog also noted Mayor Rudolph Giuliani was continuing a pattern of relying on risky budget maneuvers designed to capture one-time windfalls.

"Because it is unlikely that tax revenue collections can be sustained over the long term by soaring profits on Wall Street, it is imperative that the city initiate actions that produce recurring savings. I am equally concerned about the continued use of non-recurring revenues or one-shots, to close budget gaps," Hevesi said in prepared remarks.

For fiscal 1998, which begins July 1, Giuliani carried over several proposals from the previous year that never were achieved, including $338 million in cutbacks in entitlement programs mandated by the state, $270 million in back rent from airports, $68 million in other state actions, and $125 million in asset sales, including selling the United Nations Plaza Hotel.
Hevesi noted that Gov. George Pataki has proposed adding back $100 million to the steep cuts in the Medicaid program that he initially put forward.

And the city official pointed out that New York City still was including $1 billion from selling its water system in its financial plan, a proposal Hevesi has fought and won in early court rounds. The Court of Appeals is expected to make its ruling shortly.

The city comptroller saluted the mayor's efforts to use part of the fiscal 1997 surplus -- estimated at $220 million to $396 million -- to close next year's budget gap, cut taxes and maintain funding for the Board of Education, which in the first few years of the Giuliani Administration saw its budget substantially reduced.
And he applauded the mayor for using cautious economic and revenue assumptions, which only call for Wall Street's powerhouses to produce average earnings.

City budget director Joseph Lhota has pointed out that the city is only expecting this crucial sector to generate around $4.7 billion of profits. If the financial industry exceeds this estimate, the city once again could reap a windfall.

New York City's vulnerability to Albany's decisions was stressed by the city comptroller, who noted that the legislature's failure to extend the city's personal income tax surcharge at a special session last December posed the biggest risk for the city's 1998 fiscal year, which starts July 1.
The 12.5 percent surcharge, which expired at the end of 1996, was expected to give the city $469 million in fiscal 1998.
And Hevesi noted legislation for the 14 percent additional surcharge, which expires at the end of 1997, was projected to give the city $239 million in the second half of fiscal 1998.
Until New York City and Albany reach agreement on these issues, he said he was identifying the full $708 million in total revenue from these surcharges as a risk.
